season_note: Fruits ripen through the cold months, around Magh (January-February).
look_for: A thorny small tree with small shiny oval leaves that are pale and fuzzy underneath. Round fruits turn from green to yellow and then reddish-brown.
uses: Eaten raw with salt and chilli, straight off the tree.
Made into sweet-sour bogori achar (pickle), dried in the winter sun.
story: Many families tell children not to eat bogori until after Saraswati Puja, so the first bogori of the year feels like a reward after the puja.
caution: Sharp curved thorns on the branches. Pick from the outside of the tree.

season_note: Fruits start in Kati (October) and last through winter.
look_for: Feathery branches with tiny leaves in two neat rows, like a fern. Pale green, round, ribbed fruits hug the twigs.
uses: Bitten raw with a pinch of salt.
Pickled, or sliced and dried in the sun to keep for the year.
story: Bite an amlokhi, chew it, then drink a sip of water: the water tastes sweet. Every child in the village learns this trick once.

season_note: Big white flowers in early summer; the hard green fruits are ready from autumn into winter.
look_for: Large leaves with deep straight parallel veins and toothed edges. Fruits are big green balls made of thick overlapping layers.
uses: Cooked in masor tenga, the light sour fish curry.
Added to dal to make it sour, or made into ou tenga achar.
story: It is called elephant apple because elephants love it; in the forests the elephants and monkeys get to the fallen fruit before people do.

season_note: Most fruit comes in autumn and early winter.
look_for: A small bushy tree with soft compound leaves. Waxy green-to-yellow fruits with five ridges; cut across, each slice is a star.
uses: Eaten raw with salt and chilli.
Used to sour fish curry or made into a quick chutney.
story: Children cut kordoi crosswise just to show each other the stars.
caution: Star fruit is high in oxalate. People with kidney disease should not eat it.

season_note: Fruits ripen in the monsoon.
look_for: Bunches of round yellowish fruits hanging straight from the trunk and thick branches, not from the leafy twigs.
uses: Peeled and eaten fresh; the white segments inside are sweet-sour.
story: Leteku grows strangely, right out of the tree's trunk, so children can pick it standing on the ground.

season_note: Fruits around early monsoon.
look_for: A small tree, sometimes with spines on the trunk. Small round fruits turn dark reddish-purple when ripe.
uses: Rolled between the palms to soften, then eaten with salt.
story: Poniol is rubbed between the palms before eating to make it less sour; it is a game as much as a snack.

season_note: Fruits in autumn; the old leaves turn bright red before falling.
look_for: Look for single bright red leaves scattered among green ones. Oval green fruits like olives, with a hard ridged stone.
uses: Made into jolphai achar, sweet-sour and sticky.
Boiled lightly and eaten with salt and chilli.
story: School gates in autumn used to have someone selling jolphai pickle in paper cones.

season_note: Fruits in late spring; the dried slices are used all year.
look_for: A tall tree with glossy dark leaves. Large, round, yellow-green fruits.
uses: Sliced and sun-dried as thekera tenga, used to sour dal and fish.
Soaked in water to make a sour drink on hot days.
story: Dried thekera slices are kept in a jar in almost every Assamese kitchen; elders reach for them when the stomach is upset.
caution: Traditional remedy only, not medical advice.

season_note: Fruits mostly after the monsoon.
look_for: A thorny shrub with strongly scented leaves. Long, oval, seedless lemons, much longer than the round local nemu.
uses: Squeezed over rice and dal.
The leaves are crushed into pitika and curries for their smell.
story: One kaji nemu is enough for the whole family's meal, and its smell stays on your hands for hours.

season_note: Fruits from late monsoon into autumn.
look_for: A chilli plant with wrinkled, bumpy pods that turn red when ripe.
uses: A tiny piece is mashed into aloo pitika or pickles.
Smoked or dried to keep.
story: Elders cut bhut jolokia with a spoon and fork so they never touch it, and laugh at anyone who tries a whole one.
caution: Among the hottest chillies in the world. Do not touch your eyes after handling it; keep it away from children.

season_note: Grows all year; it is at the centre of Kati Bihu in October.
look_for: A small bushy herb, often on a raised stand in the courtyard. Fragrant leaves, purple-tinged in some plants, with thin flower spikes.
uses: Leaves are chewed or boiled with honey and ginger when someone has a cold.
Offered in daily prayer.
story: On Kati Bihu, the family lights an earthen lamp at the foot of the tulsi in the courtyard in the evening and prays for the growing paddy.
caution: Traditional remedy only, not medical advice.

season_note: Flowers in autumn; the smell at dawn means the puja season has come.
look_for: Look under the bush at dawn: small white flowers with bright orange tubes carpet the ground. Leaves are rough like sandpaper.
uses: Fallen flowers are gathered at dawn for puja.
The orange flower tubes were used to dye cloth.
The bitter leaf juice is a traditional remedy for fever.
story: Sewali blooms at night and falls before sunrise. Children used to wake early to collect the flowers before the sun wilted them.
caution: The leaf remedy is traditional only, not medical advice.

season_note: Blooms in Bohag (April-May), right on time for Rongali Bihu.
look_for: An orchid growing on tree branches, with long hanging spikes of small white-and-pink spotted flowers, like a fox's tail.
uses: Worn in the hair by Bihu dancers.
story: Kopou phul is the state flower of Assam. No Bihu dancer's hair is complete without it.
caution: Do not pull it off wild trees; buy it or grow it.

season_note: A forest giant you can see all year.
look_for: A very tall, straight trunk with no branches until high up, in the evergreen forests of Upper Assam. Winged seeds spin down like helicopters.
uses: Its timber was used for building and plywood.
story: Hollong is the state tree of Assam; the oldest ones stand higher than everything else in the forest.

season_note: Big red flowers on bare branches in late winter and spring; cotton bursts out after.
look_for: A tall tree with spiky bumps on the trunk. In spring, large red flowers on leafless branches, full of birds.
uses: The fluffy cotton (simolu tula) fills pillows and quilts.
story: When the simolu flowers, every bird in the neighbourhood comes for the nectar. It is the loudest tree of spring.

season_note: New red leaves and fragrant white flowers in spring.
look_for: Narrow leaves that come out bright red and droop, then turn dark green. White four-petalled flowers with a yellow centre.
uses: Its very hard wood was used for posts and tools.
The flowers are fragrant and used in puja.
story: Nahor wood is so hard that old houses built with it are still standing.

season_note: Seen all year around Assamese homes.
look_for: A very slim, straight palm with ring marks on the trunk, often in rows around a house.
uses: Tamul-paan is offered to guests and elders as a sign of respect, on a xorai.
The fallen leaf sheath (tamul khola) makes plates and fans.
story: Offering tamul-paan is how an Assamese home says welcome; at Bihu it is given to elders when asking for their blessings.
caution: Chewing areca nut is linked to mouth cancer.

season_note: Grown all year, often climbing the tamul palms.
look_for: A climbing vine with glossy heart-shaped leaves, often winding up an areca palm.
uses: Served with tamul to guests and at every ceremony.
story: Paan and tamul always go together, the way the vine climbs the palm.

season_note: Fruits all year.
look_for: Giant leaves on a soft trunk, a hanging purple flower bud (koldil) with a bunch of bananas above it.
uses: Banana leaves (kol pat) are used as plates at feasts.
The ash of dried bhim kol peel is used to make khar, the classic alkaline Assamese dish.
The flower (koldil) and inner stem (kol posola) are cooked as vegetables.
story: Seeded bhim kol was traditionally mashed and given as one of a baby's first foods.

season_note: Grows all year; new shoots come up in the monsoon.
look_for: Tall clumps of jointed green stems that creak in the wind. New shoots come up wrapped in brown sheaths.
uses: Young shoots are fermented into khorisa for curries and pickles.
Split bamboo is woven into baskets, japi frames and fences.
Magh Bihu's bhelaghar and meji are built with bamboo and straw.
story: Almost every Assamese home has something made from bamboo, from the fish trap to the house itself.

season_note: Seen all year.
look_for: A palm with big round fan-shaped leaves split into many points.
uses: The leaves cover the japi, the traditional Assamese sun-hat.
story: Farmers wore japi made of tokou leaves to work in the fields under the sun and rain; now the japi is given to honour guests.

season_note: Seen all year; muga rearing happens in several crops through the year.
look_for: A medium tree with long glossy leaves, sometimes with large caterpillars feeding on them in open plantations.
uses: Its leaves feed the muga silkworm, which makes the golden muga silk.
story: Muga, the golden silk of Assam, starts on som leaves. The colour of the silk comes from the worm, not dye.

season_note: Seen all year.
look_for: Big star-shaped leaves, often reddish, and spiky seed pods.
uses: Its leaves feed the eri silkworm, which makes warm eri silk for winter shawls.
story: Eri silk is spun from the cocoon after the moth has left, which is why some call it the gentlest silk.
caution: The seeds are poisonous. Never eat them.

season_note: Seen all year.
look_for: A slim tree with smooth pale bark and shiny pointed leaves.
uses: Its bark was processed into sasi-pat, the writing surface of old Assamese manuscripts.
Infected heartwood gives agar oil, a costly perfume.
story: Many old Assamese manuscripts were written on sasi-pat made from this tree's bark.

season_note: In Kati (October) the paddy is still green in the fields; the harvest comes before Magh Bihu.
look_for: Flooded or damp fields of green grass that turns golden as the grain fills.
uses: The staple grain; also made into pitha, chira and other Bihu foods.
story: Kati Bihu, in October, is the quiet Bihu: the granary is nearly empty and the paddy is still growing, so families light lamps in the fields and pray for a good harvest.

season_note: Sown after the paddy season; the fields turn bright yellow in winter.
look_for: Whole fields of small bright yellow four-petalled flowers.
uses: Mustard oil is the main cooking oil in Assamese kitchens.
Young greens are cooked as lai xaak.
story: A winter drive through Assam goes through miles of yellow xoriyoh fields.

season_note: A climbing vegetable; it has a special role on Goru Bihu in April.
look_for: A climbing vine on a bamboo frame or roof, with big soft leaves, white flowers and long pale-green gourds.
uses: Cooked as a light vegetable or with fish.
story: On Goru Bihu, the cattle are bathed and fed pieces of lau and bengena (brinjal) while people sing "Lau kha, bengena kha, bosore bosore barhi ja": eat gourd, eat brinjal, grow bigger every year.

season_note: Its branches are cut for Goru Bihu in April.
look_for: A shrub with long, narrow, willow-like leaves.
uses: On Goru Bihu, cattle are gently swatted with dighloti and makhiyoti branches.
story: While swatting the cattle with dighloti on Goru Bihu, people chant "Dighloti dighol paat, makhi mare zaat zaat": the long dighloti leaf kills every kind of fly.

season_note: Grown all year; the root is dug up in winter.
look_for: Tall, broad, shiny leaves coming straight from the ground. The root is bright orange inside.
uses: Mah-haladhi, a paste of black gram and turmeric, is used for the ritual bath on Bihu and at weddings.
story: The Bihu morning bath with mah-haladhi is meant to start the new year clean and bright.

season_note: A common climber all year, especially in the rains.
look_for: A thin twining vine on fences, with soft oval leaves and small pale flowers with purple centres. Crush a leaf: it smells bad.
uses: Leaves are cooked with fish or chicken; traditionally eaten for stomach troubles.
story: It smells terrible when you crush it but tastes fine in curry; elders say the worse it smells, the better it is for the stomach.
caution: Traditional remedy only, not medical advice.

season_note: Grows all year in damp, shady places.
look_for: Small round leaves with scalloped edges on long stalks, creeping over wet ground near ponds and drains.
uses: Ground into a chutney or pitika with garlic and chilli.
Traditionally eaten for digestion.
story: Grandmothers sent children to pick manimuni from the edge of the pond for the evening pitika.
caution: Wash well if picked near drains.

season_note: Grows all year in damp places.
look_for: Heart-shaped leaves, sometimes reddish, in damp shade. Crush one: it smells a little like fish.
uses: Made into a sharp chutney eaten with rice.
story: Its smell surprises people the first time, but many Assamese homes keep a patch near the kitchen.

season_note: Tender curled shoots in spring and the rains.
look_for: A fern in damp ground; the young shoots are tightly curled like a violin's head.
uses: The curled tips are fried with garlic and dry fish or potato.
story: Dhekia xaak is one of the first wild greens of spring that people go out to pick together.
caution: Only pick ferns you know well and always cook them; not all ferns are safe to eat.

season_note: Sour leaves through the rains; the red fleshy calyces come in autumn.
look_for: A reddish stem with lobed leaves; in autumn, fat deep-red cups below pale yellow flowers.
uses: Sour leaves are cooked in fish curry.
The red calyces are made into chutney or a red drink.
story: Tenga mora means sour mora; a handful of leaves is enough to make the fish curry tangy.

season_note: Grows in ponds and wetlands most of the year.
look_for: A trailing plant floating at the edge of ponds and beels, with hollow stems, arrow-shaped leaves and pale pink trumpet flowers.
uses: The tender tips are fried as xaak.
story: Kolmou grows wherever there is still water, so it was always there when the market was far away.
caution: Do not pick from polluted water.

season_note: Fruits at the start of the monsoon.
look_for: A big shady tree with glossy leaves; the ground below is stained purple from fallen fruit.
uses: Eaten fresh with salt.
story: You can always tell who has been eating jamu: their tongues are purple.

season_note: Fruits in the rains and again in winter.
look_for: A small tree with smooth, peeling, mottled bark and leaves with strong parallel veins.
uses: Eaten raw, often with salt and chilli.
story: The modhuri tree is the first tree most children learn to climb because the bark is smooth and the branches are low.

season_note: Fruits from autumn into winter.
look_for: A citrus tree with very large leaves that have winged stalks, and huge round green-yellow fruits.
uses: Peeled and mixed with salt, chilli, mustard oil and sugar as a winter snack shared by everyone.
story: One robab tenga is big enough for the whole family to share in the winter sun.

season_note: Picking runs from spring flush to autumn.
look_for: Flat-topped hedges at waist height in rows, shaded by tall trees. Leaves are glossy with serrated edges.
uses: The leaves become Assam tea, strong and malty.
story: Tea grew wild in Assam long before the gardens; the Singpho people were brewing it before the British arrived.

season_note: Flowers through the monsoon.
look_for: Large round leaves held above the water, so water rolls off them like beads. Pink or white flowers.
uses: Flowers are offered in puja; the seeds and stems are eaten.
story: Children pour water on lotus leaves to watch it roll off like silver beads.

season_note: Grows all year in damp places.
look_for: Big heart-shaped leaves on long stalks, water beads on them. Often near ponds and drains.
uses: Leaves, stems and corms are cooked, often with fish or with something sour.
story: Cooks add tenga, something sour, to kosu so it does not make the throat itch.
caution: Raw kosu makes the mouth and throat itch. Always cook it well.

season_note: Tender new leaves come in spring.
look_for: A shady tree with feathery leaves made of many curved, toothed leaflets.
uses: Tender bitter leaves are fried and eaten in small amounts at the start of a meal.
Twigs were used as toothbrushes.
story: Elders say a bitter mouthful at the start of the meal is good for the body.
caution: Traditional use only; neem oil is not for eating.

season_note: Fruits ripen in the hot months.
look_for: A thorny tree with three leaflets per leaf; hard round fruits with a wooden shell.
uses: The pulp is made into a cooling sherbet in summer.
The three-part leaves are offered to Shiva.
story: Bel fruit is so hard that it has to be cracked open on a stone.
